attribution_path: Category:Audio files of bluegrass and old-time music
records.description: Gus King was born in Montreal, Canada in 1875. (some sources say 1873). He was educated at Boston Conservatory of Music and National Conservatory of Music. He became a highly respected musician playing the trombone and saxophone in orchestras (including also with Sousa and Victor Herbert). From about 1915 and for 10-15 years he founded his own bands “specializing” in brass instruments and performing “all over America (and Canada)” at vaudeville theatres. One of the female participants also playing the trombone was Hazel Griffin (1885 – 1973). They married around 1921-22 but had no children. After marrying the couple settled in Reading, Pennsylvania and Gus worked as orchestra leader and music teacher there for many years. In 1951 his “Comedy Tom” was played at a concert “with Gus King in the audience”. He died in 1966.

records.description:
Frank John Ferreira (1885-1951) was a steel guitarist born in Honolulu of Portuguese parents.  Also known as “Palakiko,” Ferera (as his name was usually spelt) left the islands at the age of 15 and established himself as a musician and Vaudeville entertainer on the West Coast of the US.  His first recordings, made with his wife Helen Louise in New York, were released in 1915, and he recorded prolifically throughout the 1920s, often in duet with guitarists Anthony Franchini or John K. Paaluhi.  Records were issued as “The Hawaiian Duet,” “Ferera Waikiki Orchestra,” “Hawaiian Instrumental Trio,” and “Palakiko’s Hawaiian Orchestra,” among many other appellations.  Ferera retired from recording in 1933 to work at his delicatessen in Queens.
John Keliikui Paaluhi (1887-1943) was a Hawaiian guitarist who first recorded with steel guitar pioneer Joseph Kekuku in 1909, and along with him, was a member of the Toots Paka group.  Paaluhi toured England, France and Germany in 1911 with steel guitarist David Kaleikoa, and again in 1914 as part of Irene West’s troupe.  He recorded in the 1910s with Toots Paka, and in the 1920s with Frank Ferera’s various groups.  His wife, Franzis Paaluhi (1896-1978), played ukulele on some of his sessions and was known as “one of Hawaii's leading songbirds,” although her first ever visit to Hawaii came in 1963, after 40 years of “singing and recording Hawaiian music in New York.”

[Hawaiian Hotel, Palakiko & Paaluhi (=Frank Ferera & John Paaluhi), Brunswick 2926, recorded 6/25/25, matrix E16060-1-62/3]

records.file: File:The Jogo Blues by W.C. Handy (1913).mp3
attribution_path: Category:Audio files of bluegrass and old-time music
records.description: A fine blues piece from William Christopher Handy (1873-1958), his second published blues. "The Memphis Blues" was his first published blues in 1912, which was one of the earlier blues pieces to ever get published. His biggest blues hit, "The Saint Louis Blues" came after Jogo the following year, 1914. Handy liked to be referred to as "the Father of the Blues" but didn't invent that form of music. He did help to popularize it by getting the blues form into sheet music. Handy started his own publishing company in Memphis, Pace and Handy Music Co., with "The Jogo Blues" being one of the first scores published by it, in 1913. Pace and Handy was a successful business. Handy was a popular musician and bandleader who eventually moved to New York City and became established there.

records.file: File:Green Sleeves (2nd Chorus in self Improvisation) JasonMCH.ogg
records.country_source_category: Category:Folk music of the United Kingdom
attribution_path: Category:Folk music of the United Kingdom
records.description:
Series of 'Green Sleeves Impressionism' (Jason's Improvisation) - 2nd Chorus in self Improvisation: 
Hi, friends, did you have one type of complex that somethings you felt hard to forget but which had been growing from the depth of your heart? Oh, they are some impressions and meaningful imageries building your memories for some places, some emotional streams and some personal events.
Now, taking an online course of Goldsmiths on Future Learn Platform (though for Jazz & Blues) taught me an ability, or to say, helped me discover an ability called improvisation - to tell somethings deeply existing in my heart through music language, which I may not clearly say before in my reality. 
Why did I say 'discover...'? Indeed, when standing on the cross of a street and using phone-camera to pick up some beauties I used to think were in the past, I almost did some in unconsciousness, but rather than in music, they were in colours and lines... 

This time, by submitting two pieces of Old 'Green Sleeves' played by myself - one was a variation (creation) as the 2nd Chorus developed through a usage of England Minor and the other was a full edition with an original chorus, it and a Wheeling fingering chorus I had researched before (Green Sleeves (The piano skills abstracted from Chinese Guzheng)),  I found they - tunes and imageries were all 'in my heart and never gone' - beatifully staying there quietly, and forming my impression of UK - where I had been and what my basic understandings of 'Green Sleeves' were... No correct or wrong, now, I felt happy to store them in my heart... and in a 'room' full of memories I never disappeared. 
Now release and share some with you - my friends... please forgive my fragmental memories... but, let us breathe some new air in those colourful scenes... as if we were always together overcoming the loneliness in each heart, under the lights of 'Green Sleeves' .

records.artist: Edison Quartet, later known as the Hayden Quartet
records.description: A 1905 phonographic recording of Henry C. Work's "Grandfather's Clock", performed by the Edison Quartet, later renamed to the Hayden Quartet. The song, penned in 1876 following a hiatus in songwriting, had the most sales of any mid-19th-century American composition, possibly except for "Old Folks at Home." It single-handedly revived Work's career, although he could never recreate the song's success. It was picked up by Edison's record label at the height of its popularity. The Edison Quartet, one of the most renowned of their time, performed the song in one take in 1905. This rendition is labelled as Edison Record 8967, Cylinder 6671. The male choral vocals are accompanied by orchestral arrangements.

records.country_source_category: Category:Folk music of the United States

records.description:
Piano Improvising- 'Now's The Time' - Second chorus(A learnt & Exercised combination of both Ray d’Inverno & Miles Davis' Teaching version and Charlie Parker's original one): 
Required by my course (Learn Jazz Piano: I. Begin with the Blues Goldsmiths, University of London ) on Future Learn platform, this sound file was hands-recorded as the second chorus of 'Now's The Time', which was named by myself (Jason M. C., Han (talk) 13:40, 17 January 2018 (UTC)) as 'Panda's Dance'.
Jason, could you simply talk about your inspirations?
Oh, thanks to chances on  wikicommons, wikipedia and wikiversity! As I had disscused with peers on the playform of Future Learn, it followed the idea inspired by my mother - '有头小熊猫' (pronunciation: you tow thi-au thi-ong maw)and Ha -ppy pan-da head~  when she heard my play in her first vision - 'numberless panda heads all around the sky'(Referenced from comments in course 'Learn Jazz Piano...', 2017). 
Yes, in the second chorus, I developped it as Giant Panda's funny dance in Bamboo forest (Wikipedia introductions: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_panda; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bamboo). Indeed, in Chinese language habits, we haven't quite often use 'Giant' in front of big panda. But, it was quite descriptive and lovely, I thought. Imagining, what a situation it would be when you saw a panda in a bamboo forest! 'His or her' less cares would damage some followers and grass, but you would easily forgive the cute face and the innocent behaviors. Meanwhile, what a lovely painting that a bamboo forest with some gentle breezes embracing this 'little' creature's free play from nature...! If changing the identity that you were 'him or her', in one sunny afternoon, could taking a seat beside river in the bamboo forest with your favorite food as the material of 'a big house' from the ground to the sky release all your pressures? Oh, you can also hear some Jazz & Blue ornamentations - 'pizzicato & till' (formed by three blue notes in American Blue Scale) which could be in the analogies with panda's playing of spring water, running after fish with waves or a singing bird... 
Furthermore, the main theme in main choruses has been developped to be a repeated pentatonic motif like giant panda's strong footsteps, which was one of my researched idea somehow showing American Blues Scale's deep pentatonic characteristics. 

Thanks to your love, if...! Now's The Time to listen...
